q: This poetic form has six stanzas of six lines each followed by a three-line envoi. The end words of the first stanza are repeated in a set pattern in the other stanzas. Elizabeth Bishop wrote a famous one about a grandmother and a child. For 10 points, name this form.

This interlocking rhyme scheme, in which the second line of a three-line stanza rhymes with the first and third of the next, was used by Dante in the Divine Comedy. Percy Shelley used it in "Ode to the West Wind." For 10 points, name this rhyme scheme.

This form, used in Persian and Urdu poetry, is made of couplets that each end with a repeated refrain. The poet often includes his or her own name in the final couplet. Hafez and Ghalib wrote these. For 10 points, name this form.

This metrical line has five feet, each consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one. When unrhymed, it is called blank verse and was used by Shakespeare and Milton. For 10 points, name this meter.

This narrative form of poetry was originally sung, and is usually composed of quatrains that rhyme ABCB. Examples include "Sir Patrick Spens" and "Barbara Allen." For 10 points, name this form, which gives its name to a collection by Wordsworth and Coleridge.

Which type of poem is a lament for the dead?

q: This Titan was tricked into swallowing a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes in place of his youngest son. He had earlier castrated his own father with a sickle given to him by his mother. He was later overthrown by his son and imprisoned in Tartarus or sent to the Isles of the Blessed, depending on the source. For 10 points, name this Titan, the father of Zeus and the Roman Saturn's counterpart.

In Hesiod's Theogony, this goddess arose after Chaos and bore Uranus without a mate. She helped her son Cronus castrate Uranus and later sheltered Zeus from his father. She was also the mother of Typhon. For 10 points, name this primordial Greek personification of the earth.

This monster had a hundred serpent heads that flashed fire from their eyes and produced the voices of many animals. He and Echidna were the parents of Cerberus, the Chimera, and the Hydra. Zeus defeated him with thunderbolts and buried him beneath Mount Etna. For 10 points, name this monster, the last challenger to Zeus's rule.

Hesiod says this goddess received honors from Zeus above all others, and she was a daughter of the Titan Perses and Asteria. She carries torches and is associated with crossroads, dogs, and witchcraft. She heard the cries of Persephone and helped Demeter search for her. For 10 points, name this triple-formed goddess of magic.

This hunter was changed into a stag after he accidentally saw a goddess bathing in a stream. His own hounds failed to recognize him and tore him apart. His teacher, the centaur Chiron, later mourned him with a statue. For 10 points, name this grandson of Cadmus.

This giant hunter was blinded by King Oenopion after a drunken assault on the king's daughter. He regained his sight after traveling east and facing the rising sun. A scorpion sent by Gaia or Hera killed him, and he was placed among the stars. For 10 points, name this hunter, a lover of Eos in some accounts.

This youth was born to Myrrha after she was transformed into a tree. Aphrodite and Persephone fought over him, and Zeus decided he would spend part of the year with each. He died after being gored by a boar, and the anemone grew from his blood. For 10 points, name this beautiful mortal.

This son of Theseus and an Amazon spurned the advances of his stepmother, who then accused him falsely. After Theseus cursed him, a bull sent by Poseidon frightened his horses and he was dragged to death. For 10 points, name this devotee of Artemis, the title character of a play by Euripides.

This daughter of King Minos gave Theseus a ball of thread to escape the Labyrinth. He abandoned her on Naxos, where she was found by Dionysus. The god set her wedding crown among the stars. For 10 points, name this wife of Dionysus.

This son of Tantalus was restored to life by the gods after he was cooked and served to them. His shoulder, eaten by Demeter, was replaced with ivory. He won his bride by cheating Oenomaus in a chariot race. For 10 points, name this man who gave his name to the southern part of mainland Greece.

This man killed his mother and her lover, Aegisthus, to avenge his father. The Furies pursued him until a trial on the Areopagus, where Athena cast the deciding vote for his acquittal. His sister Electra urged him on. For 10 points, name this son of Agamemnon.

This queen of Mycenae killed her husband in his bath after his return from Troy, citing the sacrifice of their daughter. She ruled with her lover Aegisthus, and was killed by her own son. She was the sister of Helen. For 10 points, name this wife of Agamemnon.

Calchas told Agamemnon to sacrifice this girl so that the winds would blow and the fleet could sail. Artemis replaced her with a deer at the altar and spirited her away to Tauris. For 10 points, name this daughter of Agamemnon, sacrificed at Aulis.

This Greek archer was bitten by a snake on the way to Troy, and his festering wound was so foul-smelling that the Greeks abandoned him on Lemnos. He possessed the bow of Heracles, which was needed to take Troy. For 10 points, name this title character of a Sophocles play.

This priest of Apollo warned the Trojans not to bring the wooden horse into the city and hurled a spear at it. Two sea serpents then crushed him and his sons. For 10 points, name this priest, whose agony is shown in a famous Hellenistic sculpture.

This nymph kept Odysseus on the island of Ogygia for seven years, offering him immortality if he stayed. Hermes ordered her to release him, and she supplied him with materials to build a raft. For 10 points, name this daughter of Atlas.

This blind prophet of Thebes was changed into a woman for seven years after striking two snakes. He told Odysseus how to get home when the hero consulted him in the Underworld. Hera blinded him for siding with Zeus in an argument. For 10 points, name this seer.

This queen of Pherae volunteered to die in place of her husband Admetus. Heracles wrestled Thanatos for her and brought her back from death. For 10 points, name this title character of a play by Euripides.

At this man's birth, the Fates said he would live only until a log in the fire burned up, so his mother Althaea snatched it out. Later, in anger over the killing of her brothers, she threw it back into the flames. He led the Calydonian boar hunt. For 10 points, name this Aetolian hero.

This king of the Lapiths murdered his father-in-law and was purified by Zeus, then tried to seduce Hera. Zeus tricked him with a cloud shaped like Hera, which gave birth to the centaurs. For 10 points, name this man, punished by being bound to a burning wheel.

This son of Helios begged his father to let him drive the sun chariot for a day. He lost control of the horses, scorching the earth, until Zeus killed him with a thunderbolt. He fell into the river Eridanus, and his sisters became poplar trees. For 10 points, name this hubristic youth.

This satyr picked up an aulos that Athena had thrown away, then challenged a god to a music contest. After losing, he was flayed alive and his blood became a river. For 10 points, name this satyr, a victim of Apollo.

This queen of Thebes boasted of her many children, claiming they surpassed those of Leto. Apollo and Artemis killed her children with arrows, and she turned into a rock that wept constantly. For 10 points, name this mother.

This Cypriot sculptor carved an ivory statue of a perfect woman and fell in love with it. After he prayed to Aphrodite, the statue came to life. For 10 points, name this king and artist, whose myth is told in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

Zeus and Hermes, disguised as travelers, were turned away from a thousand homes before being welcomed by this elderly Phrygian couple. The gods flooded the countryside but spared them, and they were turned into intertwining trees. For 10 points, name this couple, famous for hospitality.

This king of the Rutuli was a suitor of Lavinia, whom he sought to marry despite her betrothal to a Trojan. He was spurred on by the fury Allecto and by Amata. In the last scene of the Aeneid, he is killed by Aeneas. For 10 points, name this opponent of Aeneas.

This Arcadian king ruled the settlement of Pallanteum on the Palatine hill and gave Aeneas allies against the Latins. His son Pallas was killed by Turnus. For 10 points, name this king who welcomed Aeneas to the future site of Rome.

This queen of Troy was given as a slave to Odysseus after the war. In Euripides's play, she blinded the Thracian king Polymestor in revenge for the murder of her youngest son. For 10 points, name this wife of Priam.

This goddess of strife threw a golden apple inscribed to the fairest at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, because she had not been invited. The apple led to the Judgment of Paris. For 10 points, name this goddess whose Roman counterpart is Discordia.

This Titaness gave birth to the nine Muses after sleeping with Zeus for nine nights in a row. She was the personification of memory, and poets invoked her help in recalling the past. For 10 points, name this mother of the Muses.
Answer these questions about the Oresteia.
parts: Aeschylus wrote this trilogy, in which this king of Mycenae is killed on his return from Troy.
This cousin of the murdered king was the lover of Clytemnestra and helped her plot the killing.
At the end of the trilogy, these avenging spirits become benevolent after Athena persuades them to accept a new home in Athens.

parts: This wife of Odysseus put off her suitors by weaving a shroud.
This swineherd was Odysseus's loyal servant on Ithaca.
This old hunting dog recognized Odysseus on his return and died soon after.

q: Answer these questions about the Aeneid.
parts: This queen of Carthage fell in love with Aeneas and killed herself when he left.
This prophetess guided Aeneas into the Underworld.
Aeneas married this daughter of King Latinus.

parts: This woman was both mother and wife of Oedipus.
This brother of Jocasta became king of Thebes after Oedipus's fall.
This son of Oedipus refused to share the throne with his brother and killed him in single combat before the walls of Thebes.

q: Answer these questions about Ovid's Metamorphoses.
parts: This Roman poet composed the Metamorphoses.
This maiden was turned into a heifer by Zeus and then guarded by the hundred-eyed Argus.
This nymph was turned into a bear after Zeus's affair with her, and became a constellation.

parts: This wise centaur taught Achilles, Jason, and Asclepius.
This centaur was killed by Heracles with a poisoned arrow after he tried to carry off the hero's bride.
Heracles died after putting on a poisoned shirt that was sent to him by this wife.

parts: This queen of the Roman gods was the wife of Jupiter.
This father of Jupiter was honored at a December festival with feasting and role reversals.
This rustic Roman god of woods, identified with Pan, was honored at the Lupercalia.

q: Answer these questions about the Muses.
parts: This Muse of epic poetry was the mother of Orpheus.
This Muse of history was often shown with a scroll.
This Muse of lyric and love poetry is often shown with a lyre or a myrtle wreath.

q: After her father Thjazi was killed by the gods, this giantess armed herself and went to Asgard to seek compensation. The gods let her choose a husband by looking only at their feet, and she picked Njord thinking he was Baldr. She is said to have placed a venomous snake over the head of the bound Loki. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess of winter and the hunt.

This goddess's golden hair was cut off by Loki as a prank, and he had to get dwarves to forge a replacement of real gold. She is the wife of Thor and the mother of Thrud. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess.
This god's tongue is carved with runes, and he is a skald and the husband of Idun. He welcomes arrivals in Valhalla and is a god of poetry and eloquence. For 10 points, name this Norse god.

This silent son of Odin and the giantess Grid is the god of vengeance. At Ragnarok, he avenges his father by placing a thick shoe on the lower jaw of Fenrir and tearing it apart. He survives the destruction to rule in the new world. For 10 points, name this god.

This son of Odin and Rind was born for one purpose: to avenge the death of Baldr. He grew to full size in a single day and killed the god who threw the mistletoe, without washing his hands or combing his hair until he did so. For 10 points, name this god.
This stepson of Thor is the god of archery, skiing, and winter. He is a skilled hunter and used a bone as a ski, according to Saxo. His name means glory. For 10 points, name this god, a son of Sif.

This sea giant hosts the gods at a feast in the poem Lokasenna, where Loki insults all the guests. He and his wife Ran gather drowned sailors in a net. The gods needed a large cauldron to brew ale for his feast. For 10 points, name this Norse personification of the sea.

This giant owned a cauldron a mile deep, which Thor and Tyr obtained for Aegir. On a fishing trip with Thor, he cut the line when the hero hooked the world serpent, which used an ox head as bait. For 10 points, name this giant, the father of Tyr in some accounts.

This giantess was seen by Freyr from Odin's seat, and he fell so deeply in love that he stopped eating. His servant Skirnir won her over with threats and gifts, including the golden apples. She finally agreed to meet him after nine nights. For 10 points, name this giantess.

This dwarf lived in a waterfall in the form of a pike until he was caught by Loki. He gave up his gold hoard and ring, but he laid a curse on them. The curse affected Fafnir and Sigurd. For 10 points, name this dwarf, owner of the ring Andvaranaut.

After her husband Sigurd's murder, this woman was married to Atli, the king of the Huns. She killed the two sons she bore him and served them to their father, then killed Atli. For 10 points, name this Burgundian princess, whose brothers Gunnar and Hogni were involved in her first husband's death.

This father of Sigurd drew a sword from the tree Barnstokkr, where Odin had thrust it at a wedding feast. He eventually fought Odin in battle, who shattered the sword with his spear. For 10 points, name this Volsung hero.

The pieces of this sword, broken in Odin's battle, were reforged by Regin for Sigurd. Sigurd tested it by splitting an anvil, and used it to kill Fafnir. For 10 points, name this blade, a Norse equivalent of Nothung.

This being was created when the Aesir and Vanir sealed a truce by spitting into a jar. He was so wise that he could answer any question, but the dwarves Fjalar and Galar killed him and mixed his blood with honey. For 10 points, name this man, whose blood became the mead of poetry.

Odin spent three nights with this giantess to gain three drinks of the mead of poetry. Her father Suttung had hidden the mead inside a mountain and set her to guard it. For 10 points, name this giantess.

A giant disguised as a builder offered to rebuild Asgard's wall in a single winter, aided by this stallion, who hauled the stones with amazing strength. The gods forced Loki to stop him, and Loki then gave birth to a famous horse. For 10 points, name this stallion.
These three women live by a well at the roots of Yggdrasil and decide the fates of all beings. Their names are Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld. For 10 points, name these Norse equivalents of the Fates.

One of these two wolves chases the sun and the other chases the moon. When they catch their prey at Ragnarok, the heavens will go dark. They were born of a giantess in the Iron Wood. For 10 points, name these two wolves, Skoll and Hati.

This loyal woman held a bowl over the head of her bound husband to catch the venom dripping from a serpent. When the bowl filled, the venom would drip on his face and cause earthquakes. For 10 points, name this wife of Loki.

This giant had a stone head and heart, and a stone shield. He challenged Thor to a duel after boasting in Asgard, and a clay giant named Mokkurkalfi was built to help him. A fragment of his whetstone remained lodged in Thor's head. For 10 points, name this giant.

Thor went to this giant's home without his hammer, belt, or gloves, borrowing the belt and iron gloves and a staff from the giantess Grid. The giant threw a molten iron bar at Thor, who caught it. For 10 points, name this giant, who was killed by Thor.

In this poem of the Poetic Edda, a seeress recounts the creation of the world to Odin and foretells its end. She describes the death of Baldr and the events of Ragnarok. For 10 points, name this poem whose title means prophecy of the seeress.

This Icelandic author of the thirteenth century wrote the Prose Edda, which preserves much of what we know of Norse myth. He also compiled Heimskringla, a history of Norwegian kings. For 10 points, name this historian and politician.

Odin describes hanging for nine nights on a windswept tree, stabbed with a spear, in this poem of the Poetic Edda. It consists mostly of proverbs and advice to travelers. For 10 points, name this poem whose title means sayings of the High One.

In the beginning, this great void lay between the fire world of Muspelheim and the ice world of Niflheim. Where the heat met the frost, life formed. For 10 points, name this yawning void, the primordial emptiness of Norse cosmology.

This Vanir sorceress was pierced with spears and burned three times in Odin's hall, yet she lived. Her treatment is said to have started the war between the Aesir and the Vanir. For 10 points, name this seeress.

This son of Odin rode Sleipnir for nine days and nights through dark valleys to the realm of the dead. There he pleaded with the ruler for the release of Baldr, and he brought back gifts such as the ring Draupnir. For 10 points, name this messenger god.
Freya obtained this necklace by spending a night with each of four dwarves. Loki stole it, and Heimdall fought him in the form of a seal to retrieve it. For 10 points, name this necklace.

This wife of Baldr died of grief when she saw his body, and her heart broke at his funeral. She was placed on his pyre aboard the ship Hringhorni, and she later joined him in the world after Ragnarok. For 10 points, name this goddess.

In a contest of wits with Odin, who traveled in disguise, this wise giant asked riddles about the world's beginning. He lost when Odin asked what he had whispered in his son's ear. For 10 points, name this giant.
Answer these questions about Thor's journey to Utgard.
parts: Thor and his companions traveled through this land of the giants.
This swift human servant, who raced Hugi, traveled with Thor.
This human girl, the sister of Thialfi, also traveled with Thor and was given to him as a servant after her father's fault with the goat.

q: Answer these questions about Ragnarok.
parts: This three-year winter will precede the end of the world.
The final battlefield will be this plain.
These two humans will survive Ragnarok by hiding in Hoddmimir's wood and repopulate the world.

q: Answer these questions about Baldr's death.
parts: Baldr was killed by this plant, which Frigg thought too young to swear an oath.
Baldr's funeral ship had this name.
This woman rules the realm where Baldr was held, and demanded that all things weep.

q: Answer these questions about the sources of Norse myth.
parts: The Eddas were written in this island country.
This work by Snorri includes Gylfaginning.
This thirteenth-century manuscript preserves most Poetic Edda poems.

q: Answer these questions about the Volsung story.
parts: Sigurd killed this dragon.
This smith raised Sigurd and urged him to kill the dragon.
This dwarf king was killed by his sons over the gold paid as compensation for the death of his son Otr.

q: Answer these questions about the dwellings of the Norse gods.
parts: Odin sat on this high seat, from which he could see all worlds.
This is the name of Thor's hall.
This is the field where Freya receives half of those slain in battle.

q: Answer these questions about giants in Norse myth.
parts: This giant demanded Freya as his bride in exchange for Thor's stolen hammer.
This giant took the form of an eagle and abducted Idun.
Thor met this giant on his journey to Utgard. He was actually Utgard-Loki in disguise.

q: Answer these questions about Valhalla.
parts: These warriors who died in battle feast and fight in Valhalla.
This magical boar is cooked and eaten each day and is whole again the next.
This goat on the roof of Valhalla provides mead.

q: This Mesopotamian goddess ruled the land of the dead, Irkalla, and had her sister's corpse hung on a hook after she arrived at the seventh gate. Her vizier Namtar served her, and her husband was Nergal in later tradition. For 10 points, name this queen of the Underworld, the sister of Inanna.

In the Atrahasis epic, this chief god of the Sumerian pantheon decided to wipe out humanity because their noise disturbed his sleep. His temple, the Ekur, stood in Nippur. He was the husband of Ninlil and the father of the moon god Nanna. For 10 points, name this god of wind and air.

This Sumerian god of fresh water lived in the Abzu beneath the city of Eridu. According to one myth he helped create humans from clay, and in another he warned the flood hero by speaking to a reed wall. For 10 points, name this god, called Ea by the Akkadians.

In one myth, this shepherd god, the husband of Inanna, was dragged to the Underworld by demons after he failed to mourn his wife. He spends half the year there, and his sister Geshtinanna takes his place for the other half. For 10 points, name this Mesopotamian dying-and-rising god, known as Tammuz in later periods.

This sky goddess arches over the earth with her body covered in stars. Each evening she swallows the sun and gives birth to it at dawn. She was held apart from her husband Geb by their father Shu. For 10 points, name this Egyptian mother of Osiris and Isis.

According to the Memphite Theology, this Egyptian god created the world by speaking the names of things that were conceived in his heart. He was the patron of craftsmen, and his sacred animal was the Apis bull. For 10 points, name this god, whose consort is Sekhmet and whose city is Memphis.

The heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of this Egyptian goddess, the personification of truth and cosmic order. She is often depicted with an ostrich feather on her head. For 10 points, name this goddess.

This ram-headed Egyptian god fashioned humans and their ka on a potter's wheel. He was worshiped at Elephantine and was believed to control the flooding of the Nile. For 10 points, name this creator god.

This king of the Hindu gods carries the thunderbolt vajra and rides the white elephant Airavata. He killed the serpent Vritra, releasing the waters. For 10 points, name this Vedic god of the sky and storm.

This warrior was born with golden armor to the sun god Surya and the princess Kunti before her marriage. She set him adrift on a river in a basket. Raised by a charioteer, he became a loyal friend of Duryodhana and was killed by Arjuna when his chariot wheel got stuck. For 10 points, name this Mahabharata hero.

This Hindu god of death was the first mortal to die and so became the ruler of the dead. He rides a water buffalo and appears in the story of Savitri, who argued him into returning her husband. For 10 points, name this god.
This eagle-like creature is the mount of Vishnu. He is the enemy of the serpents, whose mother had enslaved his own. For 10 points, name this mythical bird, the national emblem of Indonesia.

This demon king obtained a boon from Brahma that he could not be killed by man or beast, indoors or outdoors, or by day or night. Vishnu defeated him at twilight on a threshold in the form of a half-man, half-lion. For 10 points, name this father of Prahlada.

This god was nicknamed Samildanach, meaning skilled in many arts, when he persuaded the doorkeeper of Tara to admit him. He killed his grandfather Balor in the Second Battle of Mag Tuired. For 10 points, name this Irish god, the father of Cu Chulainn.

This Fomorian king had an evil eye that killed anyone it looked upon, and it took four men to lift its eyelid. He was the grandfather of Lugh, who destroyed the eye with a sling stone. For 10 points, name this king of Irish myth.

This woman was first seen riding a white horse that no one could catch, until her future husband Pwyll called out to her. She was later falsely accused of killing her infant son and forced to carry visitors on her back. For 10 points, name this heroine of the Mabinogion.

This Irish heroine, foretold at birth to bring ruin to Ulster, fled with her lover Naoise and his brothers. King Conchobar killed Naoise by treachery, and she died soon after. For 10 points, name this tragic heroine, the title figure of a play by Synge.

This queen of Connacht launched the Cattle Raid of Cooley to acquire the brown bull of Cooley, because her husband Ailill owned a bull that matched her wealth. She was opposed by Cu Chulainn. For 10 points, name this queen.

This Welsh bard began life as Gwion Bach, a boy who tasted three drops of a potion from the goddess Ceridwen's cauldron. After being chased through many forms, he was reborn from her womb. For 10 points, name this poet whose supposed works survive in a medieval manuscript.

This goddess died giving birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi. Her husband followed her to Yomi, where he saw her rotting form and fled, sealing the entrance with a boulder. For 10 points, name this Japanese goddess of creation and death.

This Chinese woman swallowed the elixir of immortality that her husband Hou Yi had received and floated up to the moon. A rabbit and a toad accompany her there. For 10 points, name this goddess honored in the Mid-Autumn Festival.

This legendary ruler spent thirteen years controlling a great flood by dredging channels, unlike his father Gun, who had tried to dam it and failed. He is said to have passed his own door three times without entering. For 10 points, name this founder of the Xia dynasty.

This Aztec god of rain and lightning lived in the paradise of Tlalocan, to which those who drowned or were struck by lightning went. His wife was Chalchiuhtlicue, and he is shown with goggle eyes and fangs. For 10 points, name this god.

This Aztec god ruled the underworld of Mictlan with his wife Mictecacihuatl. He is portrayed as a skeleton, and Quetzalcoatl traveled to his realm to retrieve the bones of earlier humans. For 10 points, name this lord of the dead.

In the Popol Vuh, these two brothers beat the lords of Xibalba in a ballgame and tricked them to avenge their father and uncle. They later rose into the sky, one becoming the sun and the other the moon. For 10 points, name these Maya Hero Twins.

This Yoruba god was sent by Olodumare to create the solid earth using a chain, a bag of sand, and a hen. He later made humans from clay but got drunk on palm wine and made some deformed. For 10 points, name this orisha, who wears white.

This Yoruba thunder god wields a double-headed axe and was said to have been an early king of the city of Oyo. His wives include the river goddess Oshun and the storm goddess Oya, and his followers wear red. For 10 points, name this orisha of storms and lightning.

This old magician of Finnish myth was born from Ilmatar after spending hundreds of years in her womb. He fashioned the kantele from the jawbone of a pike and sang with his magic. For 10 points, name this hero of the Kalevala.
This eternal smith of the Kalevala forged the sky and later the Sampo for Louhi in return for her daughter. For 10 points, name this Finnish craftsman, who later tried to make a wife out of gold.
This Persian hero of the Shahnameh rode the horse Rakhsh and completed seven labors. He unwittingly killed his own son Sohrab in single combat. For 10 points, name this son of Zal.
Answer these questions about Gilgamesh.
parts: Gilgamesh's wild friend, made by the gods from clay, died after a curse.
The pair killed this guardian of the Cedar Forest.
On his journey, Gilgamesh met this alewife at the edge of the world, who advised him to enjoy life.

q: Answer these questions about the creation story of Heliopolis.
parts: This self-created god rose from the primeval waters.
He produced this god of air and the two children.
His sister and wife, goddess of moisture, was this.

q: Answer these questions about the Mahabharata.
parts: This archer was the third Pandava brother, taught by Krishna on the battlefield.
This eldest Kaurava prince hated the Pandavas and started the war.
The great war was fought on this plain.

q: Answer these questions about Vedic gods.
parts: This god of fire carries sacrifices to the other gods.
This god of the wind is the father of Hanuman in some tellings.
This god of the waters and cosmic order was a major Vedic deity before Indra.

q: Answer these questions about Welsh myth.
parts: This collection of medieval Welsh tales contains the Four Branches.
This lord of Dyfed married Rhiannon.
Their son was stolen at birth and later became lord of Dyfed.

q: Answer these questions about Japanese myth.
parts: This eighth-century chronicle records the creation myths.
This grandson of Amaterasu descended from heaven to rule Japan.
His great-grandson became the first emperor.

q: Answer these questions about Yoruba orishas.
parts: This trickster orisha is a messenger between humans and gods.
This river orisha is the goddess of love and fresh water.
This orisha of iron and warfare is a smith and hunter.

q: Answer these questions about the Kalevala.
parts: Elias Lonnrot compiled this Finnish national epic.
This magic mill produced salt, grain, and money.
This witch queen of Pohjola was the mother of the maidens courted by the Kalevala heroes.

q: This survey was carried out by commissioners sent to every shire, recording who held each manor, how many plows and mills it had, and its value under the previous king. Its two volumes are called Great and Little. Its name alludes to the final judgment, since its findings could not be appealed. For 10 points, name this 1086 record of landholding made on the orders of William the Conqueror.

Its text invokes Apollo, Asclepius, Hygieia, and Panacea as witnesses. It includes promises to keep patients' secrets and to avoid sexual relations with them. Although the phrase "first, do no harm" is not in it, modern versions are recited at medical school graduations. For 10 points, name this oath attributed to an ancient Greek physician.

The jurist Tribonian led the commission that compiled this work. It consisted of the Institutes, the Digest, the Codex, and later Novels. It was ordered by a sixth-century Byzantine emperor and became the basis of civil law in much of Europe. For 10 points, name this compilation of Roman law, associated with Justinian.

Henry Rawlinson copied a trilingual inscription on a cliff at Behistun to help decipher this script. It was typically impressed into wet clay with a reed stylus. The Sumerians developed it for accounting, and it was later adapted for Akkadian. For 10 points, name this wedge-shaped writing system of ancient Mesopotamia.

In 1952 an English architect and former cryptanalyst showed that this script wrote an early form of Greek. Tablets in it were found at Knossos by Arthur Evans and at Pylos. It is a syllabary used by Mycenaean scribes. For 10 points, name this script deciphered by Michael Ventris, which has a still undeciphered "A" counterpart.

A Polish-born book dealer bought this item in 1912 at a villa near Rome. Its vellum has been radiocarbon dated to the early fifteenth century. It contains unidentified plants, astrological diagrams, and nude figures in green pools, all accompanied by an unknown script. For 10 points, name this undeciphered book now at Yale's Beinecke Library.

These documents were discovered in 1947 when a Bedouin shepherd threw a stone into a cave near an inlet on the Jordan side of a salt lake. They include a nearly complete scroll of the Book of Isaiah. Most scholars link them to the Essenes at Qumran. For 10 points, name these ancient Hebrew manuscripts found in caves.

A ruler of the Joseon dynasty and his scholars promulgated this system in 1443. It was explained in a text called "The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People." Its consonant letters imitate the shape of the speech organs. For 10 points, name this script created under King Sejong the Great to write Korean.

This language has no known relatives and is spoken in the western Pyrenees. Its speakers call it Euskara. Unlike its neighbors, it is ergative and is not Indo-European. For 10 points, name this language isolate of Spain and France.

The grammarian Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi, a rule-based description of this language. The Rigveda was composed in an archaic form of it. William Jones noted in 1786 that it resembled Greek and Latin. For 10 points, name this ancient Indo-Aryan language, the classical language of Hinduism.

Its vocabulary is mostly Germanic, with many words from Hebrew, Aramaic, and Slavic languages. It is written in the Hebrew alphabet from right to left. Isaac Bashevis Singer wrote in it, and the Forward was once a major newspaper in it. For 10 points, name this language of Ashkenazi Jews.

Inscriptions in this alphabet appear on standing stones in Ireland and Wales. It consists of groups of strokes or notches cut along the edge of a stone. It is used to write Primitive Irish and is sometimes called the Celtic tree alphabet. For 10 points, name this early medieval Irish writing system.

Sailors once measured speed by tossing a wooden board attached to a rope with evenly spaced markers overboard and counting how many passed in a fixed time. The unit is derived from those markers. One of these equals one nautical mile per hour. For 10 points, name this unit of speed at sea.

This unit is defined as exactly 200 milligrams. Its name comes from the seeds of a Mediterranean tree used by merchants as counterweights. It is used to weigh diamonds and other gemstones. For 10 points, name this unit of mass for gems.

Named for a Scottish-born inventor, this unit equals one tenth of a bel. Because human hearing is roughly logarithmic, it is used for measuring sound intensity. A normal conversation is about 60 of them. For 10 points, name this unit of sound level.

In 1804, a Lyon weaver built a machine controlled by chains of punched cards. Holes in the cards selected which warp threads were raised, so intricate patterns such as brocade could be woven automatically. Charles Babbage was inspired by its cards. For 10 points, name this loom, named for its inventor Joseph Marie.

Developed by an English engineer in the 1850s, this process blasts air through molten pig iron in a pear-shaped converter. Oxygen burns off silicon and carbon, and the reaction releases heat. It made steel cheap enough for rails and building. For 10 points, name this first mass-production steelmaking method.

A Frenchman announced this process in January 1839 after a partnership with Nicephore Niepce. It exposed a silver-coated copper plate to iodine vapor, then developed the image with mercury fumes. Each product was a unique positive image and could not be copied. For 10 points, name this early photographic process.

An immigrant from Germany named Ottmar Mergenthaler invented this machine in the 1880s. An operator typed on a keyboard to release brass matrices, and molten metal cast a full line at once. The New York Tribune was the first newspaper to use it. For 10 points, name this typesetting machine whose name means "line of type."

This man announced in 1800, in a letter to the Royal Society, a stack of zinc and copper discs separated by brine-soaked cardboard. It was the first electrical battery and was a rejoinder to Luigi Galvani's "animal electricity." The unit of electric potential bears his name. For 10 points, name this Italian physicist.

Together with Jean d'Alembert, this man edited a 28-volume work whose full title begins "Reasoned Dictionary of the Sciences, Arts, and Trades." The work was published from 1751 to 1772 and was banned for a time by the French government. He also wrote the novel Jacques the Fatalist. For 10 points, name this French philosophe who edited the Encyclopedie.

This man's 1755 work defined "lexicographer" as "a harmless drudge." He worked on it in an attic in Gough Square with six assistants. His life was chronicled by James Boswell. For 10 points, name this author of A Dictionary of the English Language.

She taught philosophy and mathematics in her native city and edited her father's commentary on Ptolemy. She was a Neoplatonist who counted Christians among her students. In 415 she was murdered by a mob. For 10 points, name this woman scholar of Alexandria, daughter of Theon.

This Moroccan scholar left Tangier in 1325 on a pilgrimage and kept traveling for almost thirty years. He served as a judge in Delhi and later visited Mali and China. His account is called the Rihla. For 10 points, name this medieval traveler.

This man's travel account was dictated to the romance writer Rustichello da Pisa while both were in a Genoese prison. He served at the court of Kublai Khan. A fellow Venetian named for the city of his birth wrote about the East in the Book of the Marvels. For 10 points, name this traveler who journeyed to China.

In 1569, a Flemish cartographer published a map in which lines of constant compass bearing are straight. It enlarges regions far from the equator, making Greenland look as big as Africa. For 10 points, name this cylindrical map projection used for navigation, named for Gerardus Mercator.

It is awarded every four years at the International Congress of Mathematicians. Recipients must be under forty years of age. Maryam Mirzakhani was the first woman to receive it, in 2014. For 10 points, name this top award in mathematics, which comes with a medal bearing Archimedes.

Named for a British mathematician, this prize is given by the Association for Computing Machinery. It is often called the "Nobel Prize of computing." Early winners included Alan Perlis and Marvin Minsky. For 10 points, name this annual award for contributions to computer science.

Eratosthenes was the chief librarian at this institution, and Callimachus compiled a catalog called the Pinakes for it. It was part of the Museum founded by the Ptolemies. Its destruction is often blamed on Julius Caesar's fire, though historians dispute the details. For 10 points, name this famous library in a port in Egypt.

This Augustinian friar bred some 28,000 pea plants in a monastery garden in Brno. He tracked traits such as seed shape and flower color through generations. His 1866 paper described dominant and recessive factors. For 10 points, name this founder of the science of genetics.

q: This language was devised in 1879 by Johann Martin Schleyer, a Catholic priest from Baden. Its vocabulary was drawn mostly from English with distorted spellings, and its name means "world speech." It gained many clubs before losing ground to a rival created by a Polish doctor. For 10 points, name this early constructed international language.

A committee led by Zhou Youguang developed this system, which the People's Republic of China adopted in 1958. It spells Mandarin using the Latin alphabet, with letters such as "x" and "q" standing for particular sounds. It has largely replaced the Wade-Giles scheme. For 10 points, name this romanization of Chinese.

Wooden tablets bearing this undeciphered script were found on Easter Island. Its glyphs, such as human figures and birds, are carved in lines that are read in reverse boustrophedon style. Only a few dozen objects survive. For 10 points, name this script of Rapa Nui.

This consonant-only script, used at Byblos and Tyre, was the ancestor of the Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic scripts. It had about 22 letters. The Greeks adopted it and added vowels. For 10 points, name this alphabet of the seafaring people of the ancient Levant.

This 1648 settlement was signed in the cities of Osnabruck and Munster. It ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire and also the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch. It is often cited as the start of the modern state system based on sovereignty. For 10 points, name this treaty.

Developed by an Italian priest and volcanologist, this scale rates an earthquake's effects at a location rather than its energy. It uses twelve levels written in Roman numerals. At level I the shaking is not felt, and at XII destruction is near total. For 10 points, name this intensity scale named for Giuseppe Mercalli.

The SI base unit of temperature is named for a Glasgow professor, Lord William Thomson. This unit is the same size as a degree Celsius. On its scale, zero is absolute zero, and water's triple point is 273.16. For 10 points, name this unit.

This man made the first reliable mercury thermometer in 1714 while living in Danzig, after earlier alcohol ones. His scale set the freezing point of brine at zero and put human body temperature near 96. Water freezes at 32 on that scale. For 10 points, name this German physicist.

This SI unit of pressure equals one newton per square meter. It is named for a French mathematician who also invented an early mechanical calculator. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101,000 of them. For 10 points, name this unit, named for Blaise.

This Virginian built a machine in 1831 using a reciprocating cutter bar and a revolving reel to harvest grain. He later moved to Chicago and built a factory there. His firm later merged into International Harvester. For 10 points, name this inventor of the mechanical reaper.

At the 1854 World's Fair at the Crystal Palace in New York, this man stood on a platform and had the hoisting rope cut. A safety brake caught the platform and prevented a fall. His invention made tall buildings practical. For 10 points, name this American founder of an elevator company.

This Milwaukee newspaper editor and printer patented a "type-writer" in 1868 with help from Carlos Glidden and Samuel Soule. He later sold rights to Remington. The keyboard arrangement he devised placed common letter pairs apart to avoid jams. For 10 points, name this inventor associated with the QWERTY layout.

This British mathematician designed a Difference Engine to tabulate polynomials, but the government stopped funding it. He later conceived the Analytical Engine, with a "store" and a "mill," and Ada Lovelace wrote about it. He held the Lucasian Chair at Cambridge. For 10 points, name this man, called the father of the computer.

This man made photography simple with a box camera preloaded with a roll of film. His company's slogan said "You press the button, we do the rest." He founded a company in Rochester, New York, and coined its short name. For 10 points, name this founder of Kodak.

Sponge divers found this device in a wreck off a Greek island in 1901. Its corroded bronze gears show it modeled the motions of the Sun and Moon and predicted eclipses. It was made around the first or second century BC. For 10 points, name this ancient Greek analog computer.

Medieval Islamic astronomers perfected this device, a flat disc with a rotating rete and a pointer called an alidade. By sighting a star's altitude, a user could find latitude and the time of day. Chaucer wrote a treatise on it. For 10 points, name this handheld astronomical instrument.

Signed in November 1620 aboard a ship anchored off Cape Cod, this short agreement bound the signers to obey laws made for the general good of their colony. It was written before the Pilgrims went ashore at Plymouth. For 10 points, name this document, named for their ship.

Eighty-five essays published under the pen name Publius appeared in New York newspapers in 1787 and 1788. Their authors were Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay. Number 10 discusses the dangers of factions. For 10 points, name this collection of essays that urged ratification of the Constitution.

This document was adopted by the General Assembly in Paris in December 1948. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the commission that drafted it. Its thirty articles include the right to life, liberty, and security of person. For 10 points, name this foundational United Nations text.

A line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands divided newly found lands between two kingdoms under this 1494 treaty. It moved a line set by a papal bull the year before. The agreement put most of Brazil on Portugal's side. For 10 points, name this treaty between Spain and Portugal.

This abbess of Rupertsberg wrote the visionary text Scivias. She composed the morality play Ordo Virtutum and a large body of liturgical chant. She also wrote on medicine and natural history. For 10 points, name this twelfth-century German nun, called the "Sibyl of the Rhine."

This man published Poor Richard's Almanack under a pseudonym. He invented bifocals and the lightning rod. As a diplomat he helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris in 1783. For 10 points, name this Philadelphia statesman, printer, and scientist.

At Scutari during the Crimean War, this woman cut the death rate in military hospitals by improving sanitation. She became known as the "Lady with the Lamp." She invented a polar-area chart to show causes of soldier deaths. For 10 points, name this founder of modern nursing.

David Hilbert and Felix Klein brought this German mathematician to Gottingen despite faculty objections to hiring a woman. Her theorem links every continuous symmetry of a physical system to a conservation law. She also advanced abstract algebra through work on rings and ideals. For 10 points, name this mathematician.

This Prussian naturalist traveled in South America with Aime Bonpland and attempted to climb Chimborazo in 1802. A cold ocean current off Peru was once named for him. His five-volume Cosmos tried to unify knowledge of the natural world. For 10 points, name this scientist.

The Philological Society planned this work in the 1850s, and James Murray became its main editor in 1879. It was published in installments and first completed in 1928. Its entries trace each word with dated quotations. For 10 points, name this multivolume historical dictionary of English.

This Swiss businessman was horrified by the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in 1859 and wrote A Memory of Solferino. He helped found the organization now called the Red Cross. In 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize. For 10 points, name this Genevan.

A pharmacist at Parke-Davis devised this test in 1912, which originally diluted a pepper extract in sugar water until tasters could not detect heat. It measures capsaicin concentration in multiples of 100 units. A bell pepper rates zero and pure capsaicin about 16 million. For 10 points, name this scale of spiciness.

Its categories are based on sustained wind speed, and a storm needs winds of at least 74 miles per hour to reach its first category. Category 5 means winds above 157 miles per hour. It was devised by an engineer and a meteorologist. For 10 points, name this scale rating hurricanes from 1 to 5.

This Serbian-born engineer worked briefly for Thomas Edison before George Westinghouse bought his alternating-current patents. He built a coil at Colorado Springs to study wireless power. His unfinished Wardenclyffe Tower stood on Long Island. For 10 points, name this inventor of the induction motor.
